DNA and Genome.intro: DNA carries the genetic information that controls the characteristics of all living organisms. Understanding its structure and how it codes for proteins is fundamental to B6.
DNA and Genome.mnemonic: Remember the base pairing rules with: 'AT the GC party' — A pairs with T, G pairs with C. For the hierarchy of genetic information, think: 'Nobody Can Get Everyone's Secret — Nucleotide, Codon, Gene, Exon, chromosome, Species'. For DNA structure: the double helix looks like a twisted ladder where the rungs are the base pairs and the sides are sugar-phosphate backbones.

sections.title: DNA Structure
sections.text: DNA is a double helix polymer made of nucleotides, carrying instructions for all cell processes.
points: Double helix — two complementary strands twisted together like a twisted ladder
Nucleotides — each unit contains a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four bases
Four bases — Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C)
Complementary base pairing — A always pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds); G always pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds)
Location — DNA is found in the nucleus, tightly coiled around proteins to form chromosomes

sections.title: Genes and Proteins
sections.text: Genes are sections of DNA that code for specific proteins, which control cell structure and function.
points: Gene — a section of DNA that codes for one specific protein
Base sequence — the order of bases in a gene determines the amino acid sequence of the protein
Protein function — proteins act as enzymes, structural components, antibodies, and hormones
Human genome — contains approximately 20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes on 46 chromosomes

sections.title: The Human Genome Project
sections.text: The Human Genome Project (completed 2003) mapped the entire sequence of bases in human DNA.
points: Disease identification — allows scientists to find genes linked to inherited diseases like cystic fibrosis
New medicines — targeted drugs can be developed for specific genetic diseases
Ancestry and evolution — comparing genomes reveals evolutionary relationships between species
Ethical concerns — genetic privacy; risk of discrimination by employers or insurance companies

keyTerms.def: Deoxyribonucleic acid — molecule that carries genetic information
A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein
A long coiled strand of DNA found in the nucleus
The complete set of genetic material in an organism
Complementary bases joined by hydrogen bonds: A-T and G-C
The monomer unit of DNA, consisting of a sugar, phosphate, and base
A change in the DNA base sequence
The twisted-ladder shape of the DNA molecule with two complementary strands

examTips: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total) — each pair contains one chromosome from each parent.
A gene codes for ONE protein. Many different genes make many different proteins.
Base pairing rules are always A with T and G with C — you can calculate the percentage of any base if you know one (e.g. if A = 30%, T = 30%, so G = C = 20%).
commonMistakes: Saying a gene is a whole chromosome — a gene is just a short section of DNA on a chromosome; a single chromosome contains thousands of genes.
Mixing up A-T and G-C base pairs — remember 'AT' goes together like 'at' the same table.
Confusing the genome (all DNA in an organism) with a gene (one coding section) — the genome contains all genes.
clozePassages: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) carries the genetic information in cells. It is a double helix made of two strands of nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine. Base pairing is complementary — adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine. Sections of DNA that code for proteins are called genes.

The genome is the complete set of genetic information in an organism. The Human Genome Project mapped the entire human genome. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein. Proteins are made of amino acids — the sequence of bases in a gene determines the sequence of amino acids in the protein. Most DNA in eukaryotic cells is found in the nucleus on chromosomes.

Mutations are changes to the sequence of bases in DNA. Most mutations have no effect on the protein produced. Some mutations change the protein slightly. Rarely, a mutation produces a significant change that alters the protein's function — this can be harmful (e.g. causing cancer) or occasionally beneficial. Mutations can occur spontaneously during DNA replication or be caused by mutagens such as UV radiation or certain chemicals.

Inheritance.intro: Inheritance is the passing of characteristics from parents to offspring through genes. Understanding dominant and recessive alleles and Punnett squares is essential for B6.
Inheritance.mnemonic: Remember key terms: 'Dominant = Determines appearance even alone (one copy is enough)'; 'Recessive = Requires two copies to show'. For Punnett squares, write the parents' alleles along the top and side, then fill in the boxes — easy as a times table! For sex determination: 'XX = female (two X chromosomes, like the female symbol ♀); XY = male'.

sections.title: Key Genetic Terms
sections.text: Understanding these key terms is essential for answering all inheritance questions.
points: Allele — a version of a gene (e.g. B = brown eyes, b = blue eyes)
Dominant — allele expressed even with only one copy present (written with capital letter)
Recessive — allele only expressed when two copies are present (written with lowercase letter)
Genotype — the combination of alleles an organism has (e.g. Bb, BB, or bb)
Phenotype — the observable/visible characteristic produced by the genotype (e.g. brown eyes)
Homozygous — two identical alleles (BB or bb)
Heterozygous — two different alleles (Bb)

sections.title: Punnett Squares
sections.text: Punnett squares predict the probability of offspring genotypes and phenotypes from a cross.
points: Method — write one parent's alleles across the top; the other's down the side; fill in the boxes
Bb × Bb cross — gives genotype ratio BB : Bb : bb = 1 : 2 : 1
Phenotype ratio — 3 dominant : 1 recessive (75% : 25%)
Probability — each box represents a 25% probability for a single offspring; not a guarantee

callout.label: Punnett Square
callout.text: Bb × Bb gives BB:Bb:bb in ratio 1:2:1. Probability of dominant phenotype = 3/4 (75%). Probability of recessive phenotype = 1/4 (25%).

sections.title: Sex Determination
sections.text: Sex in humans is determined by the sex chromosomes inherited from each parent.
points: 23 pairs — humans have 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes
Female — XX (two X chromosomes, one from each parent)
Male — XY (one X from mother, one Y from father)
Y chromosome — carries the SRY gene that triggers male development
50:50 chance — each pregnancy has an equal probability of producing a boy or girl

keyTerms.def: A version of a gene
Allele expressed in heterozygous individuals (capital letter)
Allele only expressed when homozygous (lower case)
The combination of alleles an organism has
The observable characteristics of an organism
Having two different alleles for a gene
Having two identical alleles for a gene (e.g. BB or bb)
A diagram used to predict the genotypes of offspring from a genetic cross

examTips: Dominant does NOT mean more common in the population — it simply means it is expressed when even one copy is present.
Punnett squares give probabilities, not certainties — in a real family you might get all one phenotype even if the probability says 3:1.
Always use correct notation: capital letter for dominant allele, lower case for recessive — never use the same letter for both (e.g. don't use B and b for a trait, then also B and b for another).
commonMistakes: Saying 'dominant = more common' — this is incorrect. Dominant just means expressed with one copy; blue eyes (recessive) can be common in some populations.
Forgetting that a recessive characteristic requires TWO copies of the recessive allele — a single copy in a heterozygous individual is masked by the dominant allele.
Mixing up genotype and phenotype — genotype is the alleles (Bb); phenotype is what you can see or measure (brown eyes).
clozePassages: Genes exist in different versions called alleles. An organism has two alleles for each gene, one inherited from each parent. If both alleles are the same, the organism is homozygous. If the alleles are different, it is heterozygous. A dominant allele is always expressed if present. A recessive allele is only expressed when two copies are present. The observable characteristics are the phenotype; the genetic makeup is the genotype.

Punnett squares are used to predict the probability of offspring having particular genotypes and phenotypes. If a dominant allele is represented by a capital letter (e.g. B) and the recessive by a lowercase (b), then Bb is heterozygous and shows the dominant phenotype. A cross between two heterozygous parents gives a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotype in offspring. This ratio was first observed by Gregor Mendel.

Sex is determined by the sex chromosomes. Females have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y (XY). The Y chromosome carries the gene that triggers male development. Because males are XY, they can pass either an X or a Y chromosome to their children, determining the sex of the offspring. There is a 50:50 probability of having a boy or a girl, though this ratio does not always occur in small families.

Inherited Disorders.intro: Some disorders are caused by faulty alleles that are inherited. You need to know polydactyly (dominant) and cystic fibrosis (recessive).
Inherited Disorders.mnemonic: Remember: 'Polydactyly = P for Plus fingers and P for Powerful (dominant — one copy is enough). Cystic fibrosis = CF = Carry First (you can carry it without showing it — recessive).' For carriers: a carrier has one working copy and one faulty copy — they are safe but can pass on the faulty allele.

sections.title: Polydactyly
sections.text: Polydactyly is a condition caused by a dominant allele, resulting in extra fingers or toes.
points: Dominant allele — only ONE copy of the faulty allele is needed for the condition to appear
Extra digits — an affected person has one or more extra fingers or toes
Inheritance — if a parent has genotype Pp, there is a 50% chance of passing the condition to each child
Not life-threatening — polydactyly does not usually affect life expectancy or cause serious health issues
Both parents — a child can be affected even if only one parent is affected (unlike cystic fibrosis)

sections.title: Cystic Fibrosis
sections.text: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a recessive inherited disorder affecting mucus production throughout the body.
points: Recessive allele — TWO copies of the faulty allele are needed (genotype ff) for the condition to appear
Thick sticky mucus — clogs the lungs causing breathing difficulties, and the digestive system causing malabsorption
Carrier — a person with genotype Ff has one copy; they are unaffected but can pass the allele to children
Both parents must be at least carriers — two carriers (Ff × Ff) have a 25% chance of an affected child
Treatment — physiotherapy, enzyme supplements, new gene therapy approaches — no complete cure yet

sections.title: Embryo Screening
sections.text: Embryos can be tested for genetic disorders before implantation (during IVF) or during pregnancy.
points: Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) — a cell is removed from an IVF embryo and tested for faulty alleles
Prenatal testing — amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling during pregnancy
Argument for — prevents children being born with serious conditions; reduces suffering
Argument against — embryos with 'faulty' genes are destroyed; could lead to selection for non-medical traits ('designer babies'); discriminates against disabled people

callout.label: Ethical Issues
callout.text: Arguments for: prevents suffering, reduces care costs. Arguments against: embryos are destroyed, could lead to 'designer babies', discrimination against disabled people.

keyTerms.def: Having extra fingers or toes — caused by a dominant allele
Inherited recessive disorder causing thick mucus in lungs and gut
A person with one recessive allele who does not show the condition but can pass it on
Testing embryos for genetic disorders before implantation
A genetic condition caused by a dominant allele — one copy causes the condition
A genetic condition only expressed when two copies of the recessive allele are present
Testing embryo cells for faulty alleles before implantation during IVF

examTips: Polydactyly = dominant (one copy is enough to show the condition). Cystic fibrosis = recessive (two copies needed, and carriers are unaffected).
A carrier of cystic fibrosis has genotype Ff — they do NOT show symptoms but CAN pass the allele to their children.
Be ready to evaluate embryo screening ethically — give both arguments for and against in 'evaluate' or 'discuss' questions.
commonMistakes: Saying carriers of cystic fibrosis are affected — they are NOT. Carriers (Ff) have one working allele that produces enough functional protein.
Forgetting that both parents must be at least carriers for a recessive disorder to appear in a child — if only one parent carries the allele, no child can be affected (though they might be carriers).
Thinking polydactyly is caused by a recessive allele — it is DOMINANT. This means one affected parent is enough for there to be a 50% risk to each child.
clozePassages: Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele. It affects the cell membranes, causing the production of thick, sticky mucus that clogs the lungs and digestive system. Both parents must carry the recessive allele for a child to be affected. Carriers have one dominant and one recessive allele and show no symptoms. Treatment includes physiotherapy and enzyme supplements but there is no cure.

Polydactyly is a genetic disorder caused by a dominant allele, resulting in extra fingers or toes. Because the allele is dominant, only one copy is needed for the condition to be expressed. A person with polydactyly has a 50% chance of passing the condition to each child if their other allele is recessive. Unlike cystic fibrosis, someone can have polydactyly without both parents being affected.

Embryo screening allows embryos to be tested for genetic disorders before implantation during IVF. Cells are removed from the embryo and tested for faulty alleles such as those causing cystic fibrosis. Only healthy embryos are implanted. This raises ethical issues — some argue it prevents suffering while others feel it could lead to selection of embryos for non-medical traits. Genetic counselling helps families make informed decisions.

Variation and Evolution.intro: Variation between organisms can be genetic or environmental. Natural selection acts on genetic variation to drive evolution over many generations.
Variation and Evolution.mnemonic: Natural selection in four steps — remember 'VASA': Variation exists in the population; Advantageous traits help survival; Survivors reproduce and pass on genes; Allele frequency increases over generations. Also remember: mutations are the RAW material of evolution — Random, Arbitrary, and Without direction.

sections.title: Types of Variation
sections.text: Variation within a species can arise from genetic factors, environmental factors, or a combination of both.
points: Genetic variation — caused by different alleles inherited from parents; cannot be changed by the environment
Environmental variation — caused by conditions during development (diet, exercise, accidents, climate)
Combined variation — most characteristics (e.g. height, intelligence) are influenced by both genes AND environment
Continuous variation — characteristics with a range of values (e.g. height) — usually affected by many genes and environment
Discontinuous variation — distinct categories with no intermediates (e.g. blood group A, B, AB, O)

sections.title: Natural Selection
sections.text: Natural selection is Darwin's mechanism for evolution — the process by which favourable traits become more common over generations.
numbered: Variation exists in a population (due to mutation and sexual reproduction)
These individuals are better adapted — more likely to survive and reproduce
They pass on their advantageous alleles to offspring
Over many generations, advantageous characteristics become more common
points: Selection pressure — the environmental factor that determines which traits are advantageous (e.g. predators, disease, food competition)
Survival of the fittest — 'fittest' means best adapted to the current environment, not physically strongest
No direction — natural selection is not planned; beneficial mutations arise randomly and are then selected for

callout.label: Darwin's Key Idea
callout.text: Survival of the fittest — 'fittest' means best adapted to the environment, not strongest.

sections.title: Mutation
sections.text: Mutations are the ultimate source of all new genetic variation in populations.
points: Definition — a random change in the DNA base sequence of a gene
Usually neutral — most mutations have no effect on the protein produced (especially in non-coding DNA)
Occasionally harmful — some mutations produce a non-functional or malfunctioning protein
Rarely beneficial — a mutation that improves the protein's function can confer a survival advantage
Mutagen rate increased by — ionising radiation (UV, X-rays), certain chemicals (tobacco smoke), some viruses

keyTerms.def: Differences between individuals of the same species
Process where individuals with advantageous traits survive and reproduce more
A random change in DNA sequence
A feature that increases an organism's chance of survival in its environment
An environmental factor that favours certain traits, driving natural selection
Change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations
Variation with a range of values, often influenced by many genes and environment

examTips: Natural selection requires four things: variation in the population, a selection pressure, differential survival and reproduction, and inheritance of advantageous traits.
Mutations are the SOURCE of new variation — they are random, not directed. Organisms do not mutate on purpose to survive.
When describing natural selection in an exam, use the word 'more likely to survive and reproduce' — not just 'survive'. Reproduction is essential for passing on alleles.
commonMistakes: Saying organisms 'try to adapt' or 'develop adaptations' purposefully — natural selection is entirely random; there is no intent, planning or direction.
Confusing natural selection (the process) with evolution (the result — change in allele frequencies over many generations).
Saying 'the strongest survive' — 'fittest' means best adapted to the specific environment, which could mean the best camouflaged, the most disease resistant, etc.
clozePassages: Variation is the differences between individuals of the same species. Genetic variation arises from mutations and sexual reproduction. Environmental variation is caused by factors such as diet, climate, and lifestyle. Most variation is a combination of both. Genetic variation is heritable — it can be passed to offspring. Environmental variation is not heritable.

Natural selection is the mechanism of evolution proposed by Charles Darwin. Individuals with advantageous characteristics are more likely to survive, reproduce, and pass on their genes. Over many generations, the frequency of beneficial alleles increases in the population. This gradual change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time is called evolution. Evidence for evolution comes from fossils, DNA analysis, and observed changes in species.

Speciation occurs when populations of the same species become reproductively isolated. If two populations are separated — by geography, for example — they accumulate different mutations and are subject to different selection pressures. Over time, the populations may become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, making them separate species. This process can take thousands of generations.

Selective Breeding and Genetic Engineeri.intro: Humans can influence the characteristics of plants and animals through selective breeding and genetic engineering, both of which have important ethical implications.
Selective Breeding and Genetic Engineeri.mnemonic: Remember the difference: 'Selective Breeding = Slow and Stays within the species (uses existing alleles over generations). Genetic Engineering = Gene Goes in from anywhere (any species, much faster).' For genetic engineering steps, remember: 'Cut, Vector, Insert, Check' — restriction enzymes Cut the gene; a Vector (plasmid) carries it; ligase enzymes Insert it; scientists then Check the organism expresses it.

sections.title: Selective Breeding
sections.text: Selective breeding (artificial selection) involves choosing individuals with desirable characteristics to breed over many generations.
points: Process — select parents with desired traits → breed → select offspring with best traits → repeat over many generations
Agriculture examples — disease-resistant crop varieties, high-yield wheat, cows that produce more milk
Companion animals — dogs bred for specific traits (size, temperament, herding ability)
Disadvantage — reduces genetic diversity; inbred populations are more vulnerable to new diseases
Inbreeding problems — many pedigree dogs suffer health problems due to reduced gene pool

sections.title: Genetic Engineering
sections.text: Genetic engineering involves cutting a specific gene from one organism and inserting it into another organism.
points: Restriction enzymes — molecular scissors that cut DNA at specific sequences, producing sticky ends
Vector — a carrier (usually a bacterial plasmid) used to insert the gene into the host organism
Ligase enzymes — join the cut ends of the donor gene to the plasmid, sealing the DNA
Human insulin — human insulin gene inserted into bacteria; bacteria produce insulin for diabetics; safer and cheaper than animal-derived insulin
GM crops — crops engineered to be herbicide-resistant, pest-resistant, or nutritionally enhanced (e.g. golden rice with vitamin A gene)

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: Both selective breeding and genetic engineering raise ethical questions that the AQA exam may ask you to evaluate.
points: Arguments for GM — can solve food security issues; GM insulin saves lives; pest-resistant crops reduce pesticide use
Arguments against GM — unknown long-term ecological effects; GM genes may spread to wild relatives; ethical concerns about altering life
Selective breeding concerns — health problems in pedigree breeds; reduced genetic diversity in crop monocultures
Genetic engineering benefits — faster and more precise than selective breeding; can insert genes from completely different species

keyTerms.def: Choosing organisms with desired traits to breed — artificial selection
Transferring a gene from one organism to another
Genetically modified crop with useful characteristics added
Small circular DNA used as a vector in genetic engineering
Enzyme that cuts DNA at specific sequences — used in genetic engineering
Enzyme that joins cut DNA strands together — seals the gene into the plasmid
A carrier (e.g. plasmid) that delivers a gene into a host organism

examTips: Selective breeding reduces genetic diversity — this is a KEY disadvantage that examiners want you to mention.
Genetic engineering inserts ONE specific gene from any source; selective breeding selects for traits already present using existing alleles over many generations.
Be able to evaluate BOTH methods — state benefits AND risks clearly. In evaluate questions, always reach a balanced conclusion.
commonMistakes: Confusing selective breeding (works with naturally existing alleles within a species over many generations) with genetic engineering (cuts and transfers a specific gene from any organism, much faster).
Forgetting that selective breeding reduces genetic diversity — this is the main disadvantage and is frequently tested.
Saying restriction enzymes 'destroy' DNA — they cut it at specific sequences to produce sticky ends that can be joined to another piece of DNA.
clozePassages: Selective breeding (artificial selection) involves choosing parents with desirable characteristics to breed together over many generations. It has been used to produce high-yield crop plants, disease-resistant animals, and dogs with specific traits. However, selective breeding reduces genetic diversity, making populations more vulnerable to new diseases. Many pedigree dog breeds suffer health problems as a result of selective breeding.

Genetic engineering involves inserting a gene from one organism into the genome of another. A useful gene is cut from donor DNA using restriction enzymes and inserted into a vector (usually a bacterial plasmid) using ligase enzymes. The vector is introduced into the host organism. GM crops (genetically modified crops) have been engineered to be herbicide-resistant, pest-resistant, or to contain extra nutrients.

Insulin used to treat diabetes was once extracted from pig and cow pancreases. Now it is produced by genetically engineered bacteria. The human insulin gene is inserted into bacterial plasmids, and the bacteria produce large quantities of human insulin. This is cheaper, more reliable, and does not risk rejection. Golden rice is another example — it has been engineered to produce beta-carotene, addressing vitamin A deficiency in developing countries.

Evidence for Evolution.intro: There is extensive evidence that all life on Earth evolved from a common ancestor. Understanding this evidence is important for B6.
Evidence for Evolution.mnemonic: Remember the four types of evidence for evolution with 'FADE': Fossils show change over time; Antibiotic resistance shows evolution happening now; DNA comparisons show how closely related species are; Embryology and anatomy reveal common ancestry. Darwin was brave — his theory 'FACED' controversy: Fossil gaps, Absence of genetics knowledge, Creation beliefs challenged, Evidence limited in his day.

sections.title: Fossil Evidence
sections.text: Fossils are the preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms found in sedimentary rock.
points: Evidence of change — fossils show how organisms looked millions of years ago, demonstrating how species have changed
Stratification — found in sedimentary rock with older fossils deeper down; rock layers provide a timeline
Gaps in record — soft tissue rarely fossilises; conditions must be just right for fossilisation to occur
Despite gaps — the fossil record clearly shows a progression of life forms and supports evolution
Transitional fossils — organisms like Archaeopteryx (part reptile, part bird) show evolutionary links

sections.title: Antibiotic Resistance
sections.text: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is evolution by natural selection happening in real time — observable evidence.
numbered: Random mutation gives some bacteria resistance to an antibiotic
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce rapidly
Resistance gene becomes common in the population
points: MRSA — methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is a well-known example of evolved antibiotic resistance
Practical implication — always complete a course of antibiotics to reduce chance of resistant bacteria surviving

sections.title: Why Darwin's Theory Was Controversial
sections.text: Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection challenged deeply held beliefs and was not immediately accepted.
points: Religious challenge — contradicted the widely held view of special creation by God
No genetics — Darwin had no knowledge of DNA, genes, or how traits were inherited
Limited fossil evidence — in Darwin's era, far fewer fossils had been discovered
Gradual acceptance — as genetics, DNA sequencing, and fossil evidence accumulated, the theory became accepted
Wallace — Alfred Russel Wallace developed the same theory independently, prompting Darwin to publish

keyTerms.def: Preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms in rock
Change in inherited characteristics of a population over many generations
An ancestral species from which different species have evolved
The ability of bacteria to survive antibiotic treatment — evolved through natural selection
The process by which advantageous traits become more common in a population over time
A fossil showing characteristics of two different groups, indicating an evolutionary link

examTips: Antibiotic resistance is DIRECT evidence for evolution by natural selection happening today — bacteria are NOT trying to become resistant; resistance arises by random mutation.
The fossil record is incomplete but still strongly supports evolution — gaps exist because of poor preservation conditions, not because evolution did not happen.
When asked why Darwin's theory was controversial, give at least TWO reasons: religious challenge AND lack of genetic knowledge.
commonMistakes: Saying gaps in the fossil record disprove evolution — gaps exist because fossilisation is rare (requires specific conditions) and many fossils have been destroyed over millions of years.
Saying bacteria 'develop' resistance in response to antibiotics — resistance arises by random mutation BEFORE antibiotic exposure; the antibiotic then selects which bacteria survive.
Forgetting Alfred Russel Wallace — he developed the theory of evolution by natural selection independently at the same time as Darwin.
clozePassages: The fossil record provides evidence for evolution. Fossils show how organisms have changed over millions of years. However, the fossil record is incomplete because soft-bodied organisms rarely fossilise and many fossils have been destroyed. Comparative anatomy shows similarities in the bone structure of different species, suggesting common ancestry. DNA analysis reveals how closely related different species are — the more similar the DNA, the more recently they shared a common ancestor.

Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is an observable example of evolution by natural selection. Bacteria with random mutations that give resistance to an antibiotic survive treatment and reproduce. Their offspring inherit the resistance gene. Over time, the resistant strain becomes more common. This is why completing a full course of antibiotics is important — it reduces the chance of resistant bacteria surviving.

Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the theory of evolution by natural selection. Darwin collected extensive evidence during his voyage on the Beagle, particularly from the Galapagos Islands. Initially, his theory was controversial as it contradicted religious beliefs. Over time, evidence from genetics, DNA sequencing, and the fossil record has provided overwhelming support for the theory of evolution.

Classification.intro: Classification is the grouping of organisms based on their characteristics. Modern classification uses evolutionary relationships based on DNA evidence.
Classification.mnemonic: Remember the classification hierarchy with: 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup' — Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. For the three domains, think: 'ABE — Archaea, Bacteria, Eukaryota'. For binomial names: 'Genus gets the Glory (capital letter); species stays small (lowercase)' — e.g. Homo sapiens.

sections.title: The Linnaean Classification System
sections.text: Carl Linnaeus devised a hierarchical system for classifying all living organisms based on shared characteristics.
points: Hierarchy — Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species (largest to smallest group)
Mnemonic — 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup'
Binomial nomenclature — every species has a two-part Latin name: Genus (capital) + species (lowercase)
Example — Homo sapiens (human); Canis lupus (wolf); Panthera leo (lion)
Italicised or underlined — binomial names are always written in italics or underlined

sections.title: The Three-Domain System
sections.text: Carl Woese proposed a three-domain system based on molecular (RNA) evidence that replaced the five-kingdom system.
points: Archaea — primitive prokaryotes found in extreme environments (extremophiles); lack peptidoglycan in cell walls
Bacteria — true bacteria; prokaryotes with peptidoglycan cell walls
Eukaryota — all organisms with a true nucleus, including plants, animals, fungi, and protists
Based on ribosomal RNA — molecular evidence is more reliable than physical appearance alone
Replaced five-kingdom system — Woese's system is now accepted as more accurate

sections.title: Evolutionary Trees
sections.text: Evolutionary trees (phylogenetic trees) show how species are related through common ancestors.
points: Branching points — represent common ancestors from which species diverged
DNA similarity — the more similar two organisms' DNA, the more recently they shared a common ancestor
Can override appearance — some organisms look similar but are not closely related (convergent evolution); others look different but share recent ancestors
Continuously updated — new DNA evidence regularly revises our understanding of evolutionary relationships

keyTerms.def: Grouping organisms based on shared characteristics
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
Two-part naming system using genus and species (e.g. Homo sapiens)
Classification into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota based on molecular evidence
A diagram showing evolutionary relationships between species
Domain of primitive prokaryotes, often found in extreme environments
Domain containing all organisms with a membrane-bound nucleus

examTips: The three-domain system is based on DNA and RNA evidence — more reliable than physical appearance because similar appearances can evolve independently (convergent evolution).
Binomial names: first word is genus (capital letter), second is species (lower case) — BOTH are italicised or underlined.
Know the full hierarchy order: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species — examiners may ask you to put scrambled levels in order.
commonMistakes: Capitalising the species name — only the genus name is capitalised in binomial nomenclature (e.g. Homo sapiens, NOT Homo Sapiens).
Forgetting that the three-domain system replaced the five-kingdom system — the older system put all bacteria in one kingdom; Woese showed archaea and bacteria are fundamentally different.
Thinking organisms in the same genus are the same species — a genus can contain many different species (e.g. Panthera includes lions, tigers, and leopards).
clozePassages: Classification is the organisation of living organisms into groups based on their characteristics. The modern system classifies organisms into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. Within each domain, organisms are grouped into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species. The more groups two organisms share, the more closely related they are. This hierarchical system was developed by Carl Linnaeus.

The binomial naming system gives each species a two-part Latin name. The first part is the genus and the second is the species. For example, humans are Homo sapiens. This system is used worldwide, avoiding confusion between different common names in different languages. Two organisms belong to the same species if they can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

Modern classification uses DNA analysis in addition to physical characteristics. Organisms with very similar DNA sequences are more closely related and share a more recent common ancestor. This has led to revisions of classification — some organisms that look similar have been found to be distantly related, while others that look different are closely related. Evolutionary trees show the relationships between species based on genetic and physical evidence.
